source.title: Tool Mediation Alters Refusal Mechanisms in Large Language Models
source.authors: Abel Rodríguez; Giuseppe Garofalo; Lieven Desmet; Vera Rimmer

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: It uses difference-in-means directions and directional ablation to test refusal-related mechanisms, but differs from the claim’s harmful-minus-harmless direction and tests channel-dependent refusal rather than the original intervention in its exact setting.
record.gate_note: The paper directly tests directional ablation effects on refusal and measures harm readouts and refusal thresholds. Its GCG results report attack outcomes but do not show that the attack suppresses the proposed direction; those results are recorded under fits_no_version. The behavioral refusal-rate table across prompting conditions is not separately extracted here because it does not measure the proposed direction or its causal role.
record.test_reason: It applies difference-in-means refusal-direction ablation and harm/refusal probing in a new setting (tool-mediated vs conversational requests) across 8 open models. It reports refusal breakdown under ablation (V1) and refusal at matched harm readouts (V5). The ablated direction is refused-minus-complied on harmful intents, not harmful-minus-harmless.
record.authors_conclusion: Essentially correct. Harm information survives tool mediation, but tool-mediated inputs face a higher effective refusal threshold and partly distinct neuronal contributions. Tool refusal is more brittle to both directional ablation and GCG. Much of the shift appears at tool exposure, before any execution directive.
record.recipe_differences: Uses difference-in-means directions and directional ablation, but distinguishes harm directions (harmful minus benign) from refusal directions (refused minus complied among harmful intents), compares conversational and tool-mediated channels, and intervenes from a prespecified layer onward. It does not test direction addition.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome depends on interaction channel and intervention direction. The tool-channel refusal direction is more channel-selective; refusal breaks at lower doses in the tool channel. Tool exposure and the explicit tool-call directive also affect refusal. Conversational judgments use an LLM judge while tool compliance is parsed from tool calls.

fits_no_version.finding: GCG suffix attacks broke tool-mediated refusal more often and in fewer steps than conversational refusal in 7 dense models; gpt-oss-20b was excluded. The attack is not linked to the refusal direction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under equal GCG budgets, tool-mediated refusal is more vulnerable to input-space attacks than conversational refusal.

fits_no_version.finding: Harm directions differ across channels (cross-channel cosine 0.22-0.71, falling with depth). Refusal axes fall to 0.40 (Ministral) and 0.25 (Llama-70B). Channel-selective late-MLP neurons causally dissociate the channels' harm projections in all 7 dense models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harm and refusal directions are partly channel-specific: conversational and tool-mediated inputs use partially distinct directions and neurons.

record.problems: Conversational refusal is near saturation in several models, making refusal directions difficult to estimate. The paper uses different compliance criteria in the two channels (LLM judging versus tool-call parsing), acknowledges that this may contribute to the gap, and reports low judge agreement for Ministral-3-8B (AC1 0.396). Directional-ablation dose values are presented in a figure and not tabulated. GCG uses only 8-12 intents per model. The study disables reasoning modes when possible and does not test extended reasoning models.
record.rows_left_out: The paper also reports intermediate prompting conditions, multi-turn results, PrivacyLens results, and neuron- and attention-head ablations. These were not separately extracted here; the directional-ablation, harm-readout/threshold, and GCG outcomes most directly bearing on the listed versions were prioritized.

untested.parts: Harmful-minus-harmless direction itself; adding the direction to induce refusal; general capability beyond benign tool execution; per-layer selection as in the original.
No weight-edit or abliterated released models.
GCG is not linked to suppression of the direction; no adversarial training against ablation.
No test of affine, cone or multi-direction refusal; harm-refusal collinearity does not address multiplicity of refusal directions.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct or model-variant transfer. Cross-channel transfer is not a stated condition.
Origin of the behaviour across training stages is explicitly left open.
Reasoning modes disabled where possible. gpt-oss-20b emits a reasoning segment but is not analysed as a reasoning model.

missing.what: Per-model ablation dose-response: which models break in both channels, censoring of conversational refusal, capability floor. Llama-3.1-8B is excluded.
AUROC rows for Ministral-3-8B, Gemma-4-12B, Gemma-4-31B, gpt-oss-20b. gpt-oss values are lower (0.732-0.811).
Refusal-axis cross-channel cosine profile for Ministral-3-8B and Llama-3.1-70B.
Harm displacement under tool mediation is not harm-specific: the harm axis sits at the 26th-60th percentile of a random-direction null.
PrivacyLens replication: harm AUROC 0.97-1.00 alongside a tool refusal drop.

record.verdict_notes: The ablation evidence is described by the authors as suggestive and is figure-only per model. Compliance criteria differ by channel: tool-call parsing vs an LLM judge, with judge AC1 0.396 for Ministral. Conversational refusal is near saturation, so the conversational refusal direction is estimable only for Ministral-3-8B and Llama-3.1-70B. The original V1 recipe is not replicated exactly.

versions.untested_parts: The study ablates refusal directions derived from refused-versus-complied harmful responses, not the claim’s harmful-minus-harmless direction. It does not add a direction to induce harmless-request refusals, does not report complete removal of refusal, and does not test general capability beyond benign execution in the directional-ablation analysis. Ablation is applied from a prespecified layer onward, not shown to be removal from every layer.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration experiment.
GCG attacks are evaluated, but the study does not show that they work by suppressing the refusal direction; it does not train against direction ablation.

The study compares harm and refusal directions and describes their relation as approximately, not exactly, one-dimensional. It does not test affine or cone models directly or systematically measure how many refusal directions are required.
The study measures harm decodability and refusal behavior at matched harm readouts, but does not independently intervene on harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or model-variant transfer test. Cross-channel analyses concern conversational versus tool-mediated inputs, which is not one of the stated transfer conditions.
The study does not compare training stages or training procedures; it explicitly leaves the origin of the channel-dependent behavior unresolved.
Native reasoning or thinking modes were disabled when possible; extended-reasoning models are left for future work.

source_check.notes: The ablation evidence (R1-R14) is qualitative in the text: doses, break rates and capability floors are figure-only, and the authors call it suggestive. The ablated directions are refused-minus-complied (channel-neutral or tool-channel), applied from a fixed layer onward. The AUROC rows cover only 4 of 8 models (Ministral-3-8B, Gemma-4-12B/31B and gpt-oss-20b are missing, down to 0.732). Figure 5's right-column labels are scrambled; only Qwen3-32B 0.76 and Llama-3.1-8B 0.78 are stated in prose. Rows R39-R46 should not be linked to V4. Compliance is judged by tool-call parsing in the tool channel and by the Qwen3Guard judge in the conversational one, a confound the authors acknowledge. The record's authors_conclusion paraphrase is correct.

statements.correction: App. C.7: tool refusal fails at a lower dose than conversational in every model where both channels break measurably. Conversational refusal frequently survives the usable range (doses below each model's capability floor). Directions ablated: channel-neutral and tool-channel refused-minus-complied. Figure 7 covers Qwen3-8B/32B, Llama-3.1-70B, Ministral-3-8B, Gemma-4-12B/31B and gpt-oss-20b; doses are figure-only. Authors call this suggestive evidence.
statements.problem: Overstates: the text says conversational refusal 'frequently' survives, not always. The study is filed under a 'challenges' group, but its V1 verdicts are supports (tool channel) and limits_scope (conversational). gpt-oss-20b, also in Figure 7, is omitted.
The per-model list rests on Figure 7. The text states the result for every model with measurable breakdown in both channels. gpt-oss-20b (in Figure 7) is not listed.

statements.correction: Table 3 AUROC, eight models: conversational direction on C 0.811-0.947, on T 0.758-0.913; tool direction on C 0.732-0.941, on T 0.735-0.921. Lowest values are gpt-oss-20b. Qwen3-8B 0.868-0.943 is correct.
statements.problem: AUROC 0.81-0.95 holds only for Qwen3-8B/32B and Llama-3.1-8B/70B. Across the study's eight models the range is wider.
